newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HINGIS HEADS TO HISTORY IN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS HEADS TO HISTORY IN OPEN.

text.p: Swiss 16-year-old Martina Hingis powered towards a place in tennis history on Thursday when she cruised through to the final of the Australian Open and a showdown with former champion Mary Pierce.
The world number four looked almost invincible as she outplayed veteran American Mary Joe Fernandez in a methodical 6-1 6-3 victory.
"I just played an unbelievable match," said Hingis. "I wasn't nervous at all and I played very good tennis."

Hingis's next opponent -- some would say victim -- will be 1995 champion Pierce, who was at her fired-up best in the other semifinal. If Hingis wins, she will become the youngest grand slam champion in the Open era of tennis.
Pierce beat South African 12th seed Amanda Coetzer 7-5 6-1 and said she was hungry to repeat her 1995 triumph.

"Last year in Paris if someone had told me that I would be here now, I wouldn't have believed them," said Pierce, who took three months off the game last year to overcome a prolonged slump in form and a shoulder injury.
"I was going through hard times," she said.
Pierce served aggressively and used passing shots deep into Coetzer's court to build up a 5-1 first-set lead, but saw Coetzer broke her next two service games to even the score.

The South African, who is Pierce's doubles partner in Melbourne, beat world number one Steffi Graf in the fourth round and the French diva's many fans in the crowd began to fear that her fragile confidence would once again let her down.
But Pierce held her nerve and serve in the next game before breaking Coetzer with a cracking forehand pass to win the set.
Coetzer broke Pierce's serve in the first game of the second set but her fighting spirit was gone. Pierce wrapped up the match in 74 minutes.
In the second semifinal, Hingis was even more impressive.
The Czechoslovak-born Swiss became the youngest finalist ever at the Australian Open and Thursday's performance suggested the next step in tennis history was hers for the taking.
Hingis only became a professional two years ago.
Her previous best grand slam performance was reaching the semifinals of last year's U.S. Open.
Hingis had promised to play an up-front, aggressive game against the number 14 seed, but she hardly needed to.
She hovered around the baseline slamming perfectly-judged passing shots and dictating the pace of the match except for a brief period at the end of the second set.

Fernandez had managed to break her serve once in the first set, but without holding her own. She held serve in the fifth game of the second set and saved two match points at 5-1 as Hingis angrily questioned a line-call.
Serving for the match at 5-2, a distracted Hingis allowed herself to be broken again.
Fernandez continued to grow in confidence but Hingis stepped up a gear, breaking her opponent's serve with a fierce forehand pass across the court to wrap up victory in 69 minutes.
American second seed Michael Chang was due to meet unseeded Spaniard Carlos Moya in the first of the men's singles semifinals later on Thursday.
The second men's semifinal between world number one Pete Sampras and Austrian fifth seed Thomas Muster was set down for Friday.
